summary.text: For all smaller candidates, the proof bounds the factorization to fewer than 15 prime factors (since every factor is at least 2 and \(2^{15}>28749\)) and trial division to divisors below \(\sqrt n<171\), then exhaustively checks in blocks that no composite gives residue zero. At the exceptional value, \(28749=3\cdot7\cdot37\cdot37\) and the concatenation is \(373737=13\cdot28749\), so its residue is zero.

full_proof.text:
Let the prime factors of an integer \(n\ge 2\), written with multiplicity and in nondecreasing order, be
\[
p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_r.
\]
For a positive integer \(x\), let \(d(x)\) be its number of decimal digits. Appending \(x\) to the right of a nonnegative integer \(y\) is the operation
\[
y\mathbin{\|}x=y10^{d(x)}+x.
\]
Thus the integer obtained by concatenating the prime factors of \(n\) is defined recursively by
\[
C_0=0,\qquad C_i=C_{i-1}10^{d(p_i)}+p_i\quad(1\le i\le r),
\]
and the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=C_r\pmod n,
\]
where the remainder is chosen in \(\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\). For completeness, one may put \(a(0)=a(1)=0\), although these two values play no role because neither 0 nor 1 is composite.

We prove two things: first, that \(28749\) is composite and has \(a(28749)=0\); second, that no smaller composite integer has remainder zero.

## 1. The value at \(28749\)

We have
\[
37^2=1369,
\]
and hence
\[
3\cdot 7\cdot 37^2=21\cdot1369=28749.
\]
The numbers \(3,7,37\) are prime, so the prime-factor list of \(28749\), in nondecreasing order and with multiplicity, is
\[
3,7,37,37.
\]
Its concatenation is therefore
\[
3\mathbin{\|}7\mathbin{\|}37\mathbin{\|}37=373737.
\]
A direct multiplication gives
\[
373737=13\cdot28749.
\]
Consequently
\[
a(28749)=373737\bmod28749=0.
\]
The displayed nontrivial factorization also shows that \(28749\) is composite.

## 2. Exact finite procedure used below \(28749\)

It remains to exclude every composite \(n<28749\). We describe the finite computation and prove that each of its tests has exactly the required mathematical meaning.

### Least-factor computation

For an integer \(n\ge2\), its least prime factor can be found by trial division as follows. First test divisibility by 2. If 2 divides \(n\), return 2. Otherwise test the odd integers
\[
3,5,7,9,\ldots
\]
in order. At a current odd candidate \(k\), return \(k\) if \(k\mid n\). If \(k^2>n\) before a divisor has been found, return \(n\).

This procedure returns the least prime factor of \(n\). Indeed, if it returns a divisor \(k\), all smaller possible prime divisors have already been excluded; if \(k\) itself were composite, it would possess a smaller prime divisor, which would also divide \(n\), contradicting those earlier tests. If the procedure reaches \(k^2>n\) without finding a divisor, \(n\) cannot be composite: every composite \(n=uv\), with \(1<u\le v\), has a prime divisor at most \(u\le\sqrt n<k\), and that divisor would already have been found. Thus in this case \(n\) is prime and its least prime factor is \(n\).

The actual finite version used in the computation allows 200 odd-candidate stages. This is more than enough in the entire range under consideration. For \(n\le28749\),
\[
\sqrt n<170,
\]
because
\[
170^2=28900>28749.
\]
Hence trial division certainly reaches a candidate whose square exceeds \(n\) long before 200 successive odd candidates can be exhausted. Therefore the bounded least-factor routine agrees with ordinary least-prime-factor trial division for every \(n\le28749\).

More explicitly, the bounded routine used in the finite evaluation may be written as follows. Define \(T_r(n,k)\) recursively by
\[
T_0(n,k)=n,
\]
and
\[
T_{r+1}(n,k)=
\begin{cases}
n,&n<k^2,\\
k,&k\mid n,\\
T_r(n,k+2),&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then set
\[
M(n)=
\begin{cases}
2,&2\mid n,\\
T_{200}(n,3),&2\nmid n.
\end{cases}
\]
The preceding square-root bound proves that, for every \(2\le n\le28749\), \(M(n)\) is precisely the least prime factor of \(n\).

This also gives an exact compositeness test on the range. For \(n<2\), declare the test false. For \(2\le n\le28749\), declare \(n\) composite exactly when
\[
M(n)<n.
\]
If \(n\) is prime, its least prime factor is itself, so this inequality is false. If \(n\) is composite, its least prime factor is a proper factor and is therefore strictly less than \(n\). Thus the test is equivalent to compositeness.

### Generation of the complete prime-factor list

Starting with \(q_0=n\), repeatedly perform the following operation while \(q_i\ge2\):
\[
p_{i+1}=M(q_i),\qquad q_{i+1}=q_i/p_{i+1}.
\]
The returned values \(p_i\) are exactly the prime factors of \(n\), with multiplicity. This follows inductively: \(p_{i+1}\) is the least prime factor of the current quotient \(q_i\), and division by it removes exactly one occurrence of that factor. Repeating until the quotient is 1 gives a product equal to \(n\). The factors occur in nondecreasing order: after dividing by the least prime factor \(p\), the remaining quotient cannot have a prime factor smaller than \(p\), since such a factor would also have divided the previous quotient and would have been chosen first.

Only 15 recursive slots were allotted to this factor-list calculation. That bound cannot truncate a factorization in the range. If \(n\) has \(r\) prime factors counted with multiplicity, each factor is at least 2, and hence
\[
2^r\le n.
\]
But
\[
n\le28749<32768=2^{15}.
\]
It follows that \(r<15\), so in fact there are at most 14 factors. Thus 15 slots are sufficient, including the final termination check. Every quotient encountered is at most the original \(n\), so the correctness of the bounded least-factor routine applies at every stage.

### Decimal lengths and concatenation

The decimal digit length was evaluated by repeated division by 10. For a positive integer \(x\), define
\[
D(x)=1+D(\lfloor x/10\rfloor),
\]
with \(D(0)=0\). Repeatedly deleting the final decimal digit shows that \(D(x)=d(x)\), the ordinary number of decimal digits of \(x\). The bounded evaluation allowed 28749 recursive steps. Every prime factor \(p_i\) divides \(n\), and therefore
\[
p_i\le n\le28749,
\]
so this bound is vastly more than is needed and the digit calculation always terminates with the exact value.

The concatenation calculation then begins with \(C=0\) and, for each generated prime factor \(p\), replaces \(C\) by
\[
C10^{D(p)}+p.
\]
Since \(D(p)=d(p)\), this operation appends precisely the decimal representation of \(p\). Since the generated list is the complete nondecreasing prime-factor list with multiplicity, reducing the final \(C\) modulo \(n\) gives exactly \(a(n)\).

Thus, throughout \(0\le n\le28749\), the following finite test is mathematically equivalent to “\(n\) is composite and \(a(n)=0\)”:

1. If \(n<2\), return false.
2. Compute \(M(n)\) by the bounded trial division above, and test whether \(M(n)<n\).
3. Generate all prime factors by repeated least-factor extraction, using at most 15 slots.
4. Concatenate them using repeated decimal division to determine each factor's digit length.
5. Reduce the concatenation modulo \(n\), and test whether that remainder is zero.
6. Return true exactly when both the compositeness test and the zero-remainder test are true.

## 3. Exhaustive exclusion below \(28749\)

The preceding exact test was evaluated for every integer in the half-open interval
\[
[0,28749).
\]
For clarity and to make the coverage of the finite range explicit, the evaluation was divided into the 57 full blocks
\[
[500j,500(j+1))\qquad (j=0,1,\ldots,56)
\]
and the final block
\[
[28500,28749).
\]
Thus the full blocks cover \([0,28500)\), and the last block covers the remaining 249 integers; there are neither gaps nor overlaps affecting coverage.

Within a block \([s,t)\), the scan was the following elementary recursion. Starting at \(i=s\), evaluate
\[
\neg\bigl(\operatorname{CompositeTest}(i)\ \wedge\ (\operatorname{ConcatRemainder}(i)=0)\bigr).
\]
If it is true, proceed to \(i+1\); if it is false, stop and report failure; after \(t-s\) successful steps, report success. A straightforward induction on the number of steps shows that this scan reports success if and only if the displayed negation is true for every integer \(i\) with \(s\le i<t\): the zero-step scan covers the empty interval, and a scan of one more step succeeds exactly when the assertion holds at its first integer and the remaining scan succeeds on the rest of the interval.

Direct integer evaluation of this scan returned success on each of the blocks
\[
[0,500),[500,1000),\ldots,[28000,28500),[28500,28749).
\]
The arithmetic performed at each entry consists solely of the trial divisions, integer quotients, digit-count divisions by 10, decimal concatenations, and final remainder described above. Therefore, by the correctness arguments already given, the result of the scan says precisely that for every \(n<28749\), it is not the case that \(n\) is composite and \(a(n)=0\).

Equivalently, if \(n<28749\) is composite, then
\[
a(n)\ne0.
\]
Combining this exhaustive exclusion with
\[
28749=3\cdot7\cdot37^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
373737=13\cdot28749
\]
proves that \(28749\) is the first composite number \(n\) for which \(a(n)=0\).
